title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts record safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline = 240/240 safe, guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could only change the paired outcome if the single shared candidate failed validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were invoked, rendering the paired contrast degenerate. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, quantitative outcomes, an artifact‑based failure analysis, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
High‑level operator intent must be translated into ordered, dependency‑aware device commands to execute safe network changes. Recent work explores LLMs and agentic workflows for intent→configuration translation, but text‑level fidelity metrics obscure semantic failure modes (ordering violations, transient invariant breaches, protected‑resource touches) that matter for live NetOps. Executable, emulation‑grounded evaluation surfaces such operational faults by applying generated configs to device images or simulators and deterministically scoring outcomes [1]. The generate–validate–repair (GVR) architectural pattern—LLM candidate generation followed by deterministic verification and automated repair when violations appear—has been proposed and implemented across configuration and program‑repair domains, with mixed empirical coverage depending on verifier design [2,3].

This study tests a single, preregistered estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) under a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial LLM generation per task reused across arms). Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired experiment with complete artifact accounting and a deterministically mapped analysis; (2) precise, artifact‑grounded reporting of outcomes and statistical inferences for the preregistered estimand; and (3) an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired contrast and concrete, reproducible recommendations for future GVR experiments.
sections.related_work: Executable NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop evaluation for agentic systems have emerged to reveal planning and execution failures beyond text accuracy; NetConfArena is a recent example [1]. Automated configuration repair and program repair literature documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators can enable high repair coverage for many syntactic and some semantic faults, yet verifier semantic reach remains a limiting factor [2,4]. Surveys of agentic LLM architectures, tool augmentation, and evaluation practices emphasize verifier integration, uncertainty calibration, and layered defenses as essential elements for operational NetOps automation and safety [3,5]. Work on network configuration analysis tools (e.g., Batfish and related systems) offers engineering precedent and design patterns for verifier construction and incremental verification [6]. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these lines by measuring a preregistered paired estimand in an emulation‑grounded GVR testbed.
sections.methodology:
Preregistered design and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and defined the primary estimand as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would produce a semantic safety violation when applied. The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial generation was produced per task and reused across both arms; guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. Under this contract the only mechanism for discordant paired outcomes is validator failure of the shared candidate or a validator‑triggered repair that changes the final configuration.

Task corpus and sampling: The planned sample was N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks executed as paired episodes (planned episodes = 480). Task composition: in‑distribution = 144, distribution‑shift = 48 (novel topologies/vendors held out from the generator), adversarial‑prompt = 48 (adversarial prompts generated under a preregistered adversary protocol). Tasks were generated deterministically and include explicit intent, initial state, required command sequences, and preserved‑field constraints.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution declared model gpt-5-mini. The deterministic verifier was a black‑box deterministic_netops_validator (guarded pipeline). The adapter family constrained provider calls so that exactly one shared initial generation per task was produced; the guarded arm had up to one repair call if the validator signaled a violation.

Scoring and analysis plan: The scorer emitted a binary final outcome (safe/unsafe) based on deterministic emulation and invariant checks. The primary analysis used a paired binary estimator with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and a paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Predeclared sensitivity channels included flags for verifier–simulator inconsistencies and infra failures; the retry policy permitted up to two infra retries per task. All analysis parameters were fixed in the preregistration.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per preregistration. Planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; complete_pair_count = 240. Provider call accounting is consistent with one shared initial generation per task (hosted model calls = 240; model_calls_used = 240). No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Baseline successes = 240/240 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0); guarded successes = 240/240 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). The paired contingency table is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied across the guarded episodes. Representative validator traces record per‑task difficulty labels and final_state snapshots showing that each shared candidate satisfied the verifier checks; therefore baseline and guarded final configurations were identical for all tasks and subgroups. Planned sensitivity analyses for verifier–simulator mismatches or infra failures were unused because no such flags were raised.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only affect the paired outcome if the single shared candidate fails deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair is applied. In this run every shared initial generation passed deterministic validation and zero repairs were invoked; consequently the guarded arm could not produce discordant outcomes and the paired contrast is degenerate. This outcome is an artifact of the interaction between the paired estimand and the shared_initial_candidate contract rather than evidence that validation is redundant in principle.

Design implications and recommendations: To obtain informative paired contrasts in future GVR evaluations, consider at least one of the following, depending on the causal estimand of interest: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm (so generator variability is not suppressed by reuse), (B) increase adversary strength or diversify adversary seeds to create more initial candidate failures for the validator to detect, or (C) expand the repair budget (permit multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair traces to study repair search behavior. Improving verifier semantic coverage (more invariant classes and cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes) will also increase opportunities to exercise repair logic.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is constrained by the shared_initial_candidate contract (explicit design choice documented in the preregistration), which restricts causal interpretation of the guarded intervention. Construct validity depends on verifier coverage: deterministic checks encode a finite rule set and may leave semantic fault classes undetected. External validity is limited by the synthetic, emulation‑grounded task corpus and a single tested model; generalization to production multi‑vendor deployments and other models is not established. Conclusion validity here is limited by the realized baseline unsafe rate = 0, which prevents detection of any verifier benefit under the executed contract.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline using declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier under shared_initial_candidate semantics. All 240 paired tasks produced safe final configurations under both the LLM‑only and guarded arms, yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The degenerate paired outcome is explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with each shared candidate passing deterministic validation, which prevented any validator‑triggered repair or paired discordance. We present artifact‑grounded recommendations—alter generation semantics, increase adversary strength, enlarge repair budgets, and improve verifier semantic coverage—to design future GVR evaluations that can produce informative paired contrasts about verifier benefit. The archived execution and analysis artifacts provide a reproducible record of the run and of the design decisions that produced the null paired contrast.

disclosure_statement: Declared model and orchestration: execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter family (hosted_netops_gvr_v1). Guarded pipeline and repair contract: deterministic verifier used (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); guarded episodes were permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task under the preregistered adapter contract. Preregistration and master prompt: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature review, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting reported here occurred autonomously after the lock. Generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore, under the executed contract, paired divergences could only arise if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Archived artifacts: execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest, task manifests, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis summaries) are included in the study artifact bundle for reproducibility and inspection. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
